name: canonical_json_key_rejects_v1
description: Object keys that every implementation must REFUSE, with the typed reason code each yields. ARM-48 resolves DISC-052. Two rules: byte-identical duplicate keys have no canonical meaning and are refused as canonical.duplicate-key; keys outside the ASCII repertoire are refused as canonical.key-repertoire-unsupported, which makes Unicode canonical equivalence impossible by construction rather than something two implementations must detect identically. Both rules apply on the encode path and the strict-decode path, at every depth. This constrains KEYS only; string VALUES keep full Unicode.

cases.note: Before ARM-48 Go emitted both bindings and Swift collapsed them.
The original DISC-052 pair. Byte-distinct, renders alike. Refused because neither key is ASCII, so the equivalence question never arises.
A single non-ASCII key is refused on its own.
One non-ASCII byte anywhere in the key is enough.

accepted_for_contrast.note: Distinct ASCII keys, including the empty key, still encode. A guard that refused everything would satisfy the reject cases while breaking every real object.
String VALUES keep full Unicode; only keys are constrained.

escaped_key_documents.why: These cases carry whole DOCUMENTS rather than key strings, because the earlier cases could not express escaped spelling at all. A key written with a JSON escape decodes to the same key as its literal spelling, so identity must be taken from the DECODED value. A scanner that compared raw bytes instead would let an escaped key evade both rules: BSu0061 would not match a literal a for duplicate detection, and BSu00e9 would look like pure ASCII and pass the repertoire restriction. Both implementations must return the SAME typed code for these bytes.

cases.note: BSu0061 decodes to a, so this binds a twice.
BSu00e9 decodes to a non-ASCII scalar. The raw bytes are all ASCII, which is exactly why raw-byte identity would miss it.
The DISC-052 pair in escaped spelling. The repertoire rule fires before duplicate detection, so the code is the repertoire one on both sides.
Positive control: BS/ decodes to /, which is ASCII and unique, so it must be ACCEPTED. A scanner that refused every escaped key would satisfy the cases above while breaking legitimate input.
